cover.title: 40 Most Asked React Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: 40 questions in 10 themed pages, 4 per page
cover.tagline: For React developers preparing for interviews: a short answer, key points and a visual for every question, ending with a cheatsheet of the rules interviewers probe most.

blocks.q: Q1. What is JSX and how does it become JavaScript?
a_bullets: JSX is XML-like syntax that a compiler turns into ==jsx()== calls returning plain element objects.
Browsers can't read JSX, so a build step compiles it
An element is a cheap object: type, props, children
Anything inside `{}` is an ordinary JS expression

blocks.q: Q2. What is the virtual DOM and why does React use it?
a_bullets: The ==virtual DOM== is a lightweight element tree that React diffs to minimize real DOM writes.
Each update builds a fresh tree in memory
Diffing finds the smallest set of changes
Only changed nodes get written to the DOM

blocks.q: Q3. What is the difference between rendering and committing?
a_bullets: Render is a **pure** calculation of the next UI; commit is where the DOM is touched.
Render phase calls components, with no side effects
Commit phase writes the DOM, then runs effects
Render can be paused or redone; commit cannot
example_code: commit: write DOM, run layout fx

blocks.q: Q4. Why can't a component return multiple root elements, and what are Fragments?
a_bullets: A component returns one value, so siblings need one parent; a ==Fragment== groups them without an extra DOM node.
JSX compiles to one jsx() call, so one root
`<>...</>` adds no wrapper div to the DOM
Use `<Fragment key=...>` when rendering lists

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: JSX is sugar for jsx() calls. Render is pure, commit touches the DOM. Fragments avoid extra nodes.

blocks.q: Q5. What is the difference between a function component and a class component?
a_bullets: Function components use ==hooks==; class components use `this` and lifecycle methods.
Hooks replace lifecycle methods like `componentDidMount`
No `this` binding; classes only for error boundaries

blocks.q: Q6. What are props and why are they read-only?
a_bullets: Props are ==inputs== a parent passes down; the child never changes them.
Data flows **one way**; same props, same output
To change data, call a parent callback

blocks.q: Q7. What is the difference between props and state?
a_bullets: Props are passed in and immutable; ==state== is owned and set via its setter.
Props from parent; state lives inside
Setter re-renders; lift state up for siblings

blocks.q: Q8. What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components?
a_bullets: Controlled input value comes from ==state==; uncontrolled keeps it in the DOM, read by ref.
Controlled: `value` + `onChange`; suits live validation
Uncontrolled: `ref.current.value`, `defaultValue`; simple forms

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Hooks components are the default. Props flow down, **read-only**; state is owned. Controlled inputs make state the source of truth.

blocks.q: Q9. How does useState work and what does it return?
a_bullets: It returns a pair, `[value, setter]`, and the value is a ==snapshot== for that render.
Each render sees its own fixed value
The setter schedules a new render
Initial value is used only on mount

blocks.q: Q10. Why is setState asynchronous, and what is batching?
a_bullets: React queues updates and applies them together in ==one re-render== (batching).
Fewer renders means faster screens
State changes only on the next render
React 18 batches in timeouts and promises too

blocks.q: Q11. What is the difference between setCount(count + 1) and setCount(c => c + 1)?
a_bullets: The ==functional updater== gets the latest queued value, so it never uses a stale count.
`count + 1` reads this render's snapshot
Use the updater when the new value depends on the old
Three updater calls add 3 in one batch

blocks.q: Q12. Why must you never mutate state directly?
a_bullets: React compares by reference, so a mutated object keeps the ==same reference== and skips the render.
Always pass a new array or object
Copy with spread, `map` or `filter`
Mutation also breaks memo and effect deps

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: State is a per-render snapshot. Updates are batched into one render. Use updaters for dependent changes and always copy, never mutate.

blocks.q: Q13. How does useEffect map to componentDidMount, DidUpdate and WillUnmount?
a_bullets: One ==useEffect== covers all three: its body runs after render, and its returned cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount.
Mount: runs once after the first render
Update: reruns whenever a dependency changes
Unmount: the cleanup function fires

blocks.q: Q14. What does the dependency array do, and what happens with [], no array, or missing deps?
a_bullets: React reruns the effect only when a listed value changed since the last render (compared with Object.is).
`[]` runs once; no array runs after **every** render
Missing deps leave a **stale closure** with old values
Lint rule exhaustive-deps catches forgotten dependencies

blocks.q: Q15. How do you clean up side effects such as timers, subscriptions and fetches?
a_bullets: Return a ==cleanup function== from the effect; React calls it before rerunning and on unmount.
Timers: `clearInterval`; subscriptions: unsubscribe
Fetches: abort with an **AbortController**
Skipping cleanup causes leaks and race conditions

blocks.q: Q16. What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?
a_bullets: `useEffect` runs ==after paint==, while `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously **before** paint, right after DOM updates.
Use useLayoutEffect to measure the DOM and adjust
It prevents visible flicker from a post-paint change
Default to useEffect; layout blocks painting

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Effects sync with the outside world: list every dependency, return a cleanup, and reach for useLayoutEffect only to measure before paint.

blocks.q: Q17. How does React's reconciliation (diffing) algorithm work?
a_bullets: React compares the old and new element trees by ==type== and position, using O(n) heuristics instead of a full tree diff.
Different type: unmount the subtree, mount a fresh one
Same type: keep the instance, update changed props
Lists are matched by key, else by position

blocks.q: Q18. Why do lists need keys, and what makes a good key?
a_bullets: A ==key== gives each item a stable identity so React can match items between renders.
Best key: a stable unique ID from your data
Keys only need to be unique among siblings
Never use Math.random(); it remounts every render

blocks.q: Q19. Why is using array index as a key a problem?
a_bullets: On reorder or insert, indexes shift, so ==state and input values== stick to the wrong item.
Prepend one item and every row gets mismatched
Typed input text stays at the position, not the item
Index is safe only for static, never-reordered lists
example_code: // rows [A, B], each has an input
// key=0 is now X, shows A's text

blocks.q: Q20. How can changing a key be used to reset a component?
a_bullets: A new ==key== makes React unmount the old instance and mount a fresh one with initial state.
All state resets with no extra code
Cleaner than syncing props to state in an effect
The key can be any value, like a userId

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: React diffs by **type** and position; keys give list items identity. Use stable IDs, never the index for dynamic lists, and change a key to reset state.

blocks.q: Q21. What is the Context API and what problem does it solve?
a_bullets: Context lets a ==Provider== publish a value that any descendant reads with `useContext`, skipping **prop drilling**.
Good for theme, locale, current user
Consumers read the nearest Provider above them
No Provider found means the default value

blocks.q: Q22. What are the performance pitfalls of Context?
a_bullets: When the Provider value changes, ==every consumer== re-renders, even if it uses only part of it.
A new object literal each render triggers it
**Memoize** the value with `useMemo`
Split into several smaller contexts by update rate

blocks.q: Q23. What is useRef and how does it differ from useState?
a_bullets: `useRef` returns a stable object whose mutable ==.current== survives renders, and changing it **never** re-renders.
useState change: schedules a re-render
useRef change: silent, no render
Never read or write .current during render

blocks.q: Q24. When should you use refs, and what is forwardRef?
a_bullets: Use refs as an escape hatch for the DOM, and ==forwardRef== lets a child pass its DOM node up to a parent ref.
Focus, scroll, and measuring elements
Wrapping third-party libraries and timer IDs
React 19 accepts ref as a plain prop

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Context skips drilling but re-renders all consumers, so memoize the value and split contexts. Refs hold mutable values without rendering; forwardRef exposes a child's DOM node.

blocks.q: Q25. What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
a_bullets: `useMemo` caches a computed ==value==; `useCallback` caches a ==function identity==.
`useCallback(fn, deps)` equals `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`
Both recompute only when a dependency changes
Stable identity matters for memo children and effects

blocks.q: Q26. What does React.memo do and when does it fail?
a_bullets: `React.memo` skips a re-render when the props are ==shallow-equal== to last time.
Fails when props are **new** objects or functions each render
Fix with useMemo, useCallback or primitive props
Inline JSX children are new objects every render

blocks.q: Q27. When should you not use useMemo or useCallback?
a_bullets: Skip them when the work is cheap, because memoizing has its own ==cost==.
Every render still compares deps and stores the cache
Useless if the child is not memo'd
Measure with the Profiler before adding either
example_code: // just write: const n = a + b;

blocks.q: Q28. What does the React Compiler change about manual memoization?
a_bullets: The ==React Compiler== memoizes components and values automatically at build time, so hand-written hooks are rarely needed.
Build-time plugin; code must follow the Rules of React
It skips components that break the rules
Keep useMemo for expensive work or effect deps

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: useMemo caches values, useCallback caches functions, memo skips renders. Measure first; the Compiler automates the rest.

blocks.q: Q29. What is a custom hook and what rules must it follow?
a_bullets: A custom hook is a function starting with ==use== that calls other hooks to share stateful logic.
Name must start with `use`
Call hooks only at its top level
Each caller gets its own separate state

blocks.q: Q30. What are the Rules of Hooks and why do they exist?
a_bullets: Call hooks only at the top level, because React matches them by ==call order== each render.
No hooks inside loops, conditions or nested functions
Only call from components or custom hooks
A skipped hook shifts every later hook's slot

blocks.q: Q31. How would you find and fix unnecessary re-renders?
a_bullets: Record with the ==React DevTools Profiler==, then cut the renders it flags.
Move state down into the component using it
Wrap children in `memo` with stable props
Stabilise props with `useCallback` and `useMemo`
example_code: } // state lives here, not in App

blocks.q: Q32. How do code splitting, lazy and virtualization improve performance?
a_bullets: They ship and render less: ==split bundles== load on demand and ==windowing== draws only visible rows.
`React.lazy` plus dynamic `import()` defers code
Wrap lazy parts in Suspense with a fallback
Windowing mounts only rows on screen, not 10,000

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Hooks run in a fixed order, so keep them top level. Profile first, then move state down, memo, split and window.

blocks.q: Q33. What is an error boundary and what errors does it not catch?
a_bullets: A class component that catches errors thrown while ==rendering== its children and shows a fallback instead of a blank screen.
Uses `getDerivedStateFromError` to flip to fallback state.
Misses **event handlers**, async code and SSR.
Only classes can be boundaries; no hook exists.

blocks.q: Q34. How do you implement a fallback UI and recover from an error?
a_bullets: Render a fallback from the boundary's error state, then ==reset== that state on retry or when a key changes.
`fallbackRender` receives the error and `resetErrorBoundary`.
Changing `resetKeys` clears the error automatically.
`react-error-boundary` saves writing the class.

blocks.q: Q35. What is Suspense and how does it work with lazy loading and data?
a_bullets: A component ==suspends== while its code or data is pending, and the nearest Suspense boundary above it shows the fallback.
Works with `lazy` imports out of the box.
Data needs a Suspense-aware library or `use(promise)`.
Wrap siblings together to avoid popping spinners.

blocks.q: Q36. What do useTransition and useDeferredValue do?
a_bullets: Both mark an update as ==non-urgent==, so React keeps typing and clicks responsive while heavy rendering waits.
`useTransition` wraps a setState you control.
`useDeferredValue` lags a value you only receive.
Urgent updates interrupt the slow render.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Boundaries catch **render** errors only; Suspense waits on code and data; transitions keep input snappy.

blocks.q: Q37. What are React Server Components and how do they differ from client components?
a_bullets: ==Server Components== run only on the server, sending rendered output, never their JS.
Zero client JS
Can `await` data or query the DB
`'use client'` marks where interactivity starts

blocks.q: Q38. What is the difference between SSR, SSG and Server Components?
a_bullets: SSR and SSG make ==HTML== per request or at build; Server Components ==never ship== to the client.
SSR: per request, then hydrated
SSG: once at build time
RSC: pairs with either, streams payload

blocks.q: Q39. How do you test a React component with React Testing Library?
a_bullets: ==Render==, query like a user, use `userEvent`, assert ==behavior==, not implementation.
Query by role or label, not class
`await userEvent.click` simulates real input
Never assert on state or props

blocks.q: Q40. How do you test hooks and async behavior?
a_bullets: Use ==renderHook== for hooks, ==findBy== or ==waitFor== for async, MSW for network.
`findBy*` retries until element appears
`waitFor` retries assertion until it passes
MSW intercepts fetch at network layer

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.text: Server Components cut client JS; `'use client'` opts in. Test what users see.

Copy arrays and objects; ==functional updater== if dependent

blocks.title: INTERVIEW TAKEAWAY:
blocks.text: Pure render, immutable state, honest deps, stable keys, measured memo.

caption.text:
40 React interview questions they will ask you. 🎯

I grouped them into ten themes so you can prep in order:

📝 JSX and rendering
🧩 Components and props
🔁 State and useState
⚡ useEffect and lifecycle
🔑 Keys and reconciliation
🌐 Context and refs
🧠 useMemo, useCallback and memo
🪝 Custom hooks and performance
🛡️ Error boundaries and Suspense
🖥️ Server components and testing

Every answer has a short direct answer you can say out loud, the key points interviewers listen for, and a visual to help it stick. There's a cheatsheet page at the end for the night before.

Save this for your next interview prep session and send it to a friend who is job hunting.

Which of the 40 do you find hardest? Tell me in the comments 👇

Comment “react” to get all the answers as a PDF.
